rationale: Economically coherent conditional twist on the net-debt-issuance/external-financing anomaly, but the indicator zeroes out all non-burning firms so the spread partly compares "distressed high issuers" against an undifferentiated mass of zeros, and the incremental content beyond the known debt-issuance effect may be thin.

The expected positive sign bets against the well-documented negative debt-issuance/external-financing relation using *gross* dltis (which largely proxies for leverage and rollover intensity rather than net financing access), and the zero-masking of non-deficit firms makes the sorted spread hard to interpret if the sign does come out positive.

Conditioning on lt > at restricts the non-zero signal to the ~1-3% negative-book-equity tail, so the long portfolio will be tiny and unstable while the rest of the universe sits at exactly zero — a coverage/degeneracy problem that will dominate any economic content.

This is close to a direct rediscovery of the net share issuance anomaly combined with the already-published result that the issuance effect is concentrated among unprofitable/financially-constrained firms, so a negative slope would confirm known findings rather than reveal a new interaction.

Dividend-paying firms with an accumulated deficit are a genuinely interesting and under-studied conditioning cell and the smoothed payout ratio is sensibly constructed, though coverage of the non-zero cell will be small and part of any positive slope may simply reproduce the dividend-yield premium.

The MIN construction is creative but internally leaky — since dltr ≥ 0, MIN reduces to net equity issuance whenever that term is negative, so the short leg is populated by levered *repurchasers* rather than non-recapitalizers, which contradicts the stated mechanism and works against the buyback anomaly's known sign.
